q-161551.name: Question 1
q-161551.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14231356/assets/6e5cb856069061be9b877753ce6c373ee9191547fce8750e9c2a8b073b99ceb0.png)

Given that $R$ is the type II region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}V=$
q-161551.worked_solution:
For a type II region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type II region enclosed between the back surface $x={u}_{1}(y,z)=1$ and the front surface $x={u}_{2}(y,z)=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14231356/assets/e5779dc92c875bef280425ed24a17cfb53f9f2a9736292a92ccdb988044237a6.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,1\le x\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $yz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-{y}^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14231356/assets/00f2847a8e4c927a1c6631f4aef03c57b9d28f18341b268182501ada07225382.png)

Hence, $D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-{y}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{y}^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡z[x]_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

For a type II region R with projection D onto the yz-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function f(x,y,z) over R is given by

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA.

We consider the region R as a type II region enclosed between the back surface x=u1(y,z)=1 and the front surface x=u2(y,z)=2.

So, the region R is given by

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,1≤x≤2}.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type I plane region in the yz-plane with the upper curve

z=1−y2.

Hence, D={(y,z):0≤y≤1,0≤z≤1−y2}.

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

∭Rsin⁡zdV=∬D[∫12sin⁡zdx]dA=∫01∫01−y2[∫12sin⁡zdx]dzdy=∫01∫01−y2sin⁡z[x]x=1x=2dzdy=∫01∫01−y2sin⁡zdzdy

q-161570.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$

q-161571.name: Question 3
q-161571.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2z}}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 3,\,y\le z\le y+1\}.
$$
q-161571.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2z}}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{4}[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{2z}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{4}(2z-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{2}z\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{2}z\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{y}^{y+1}\frac{1}{2}z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{4}[{z}^{2}]_{z=y}^{z=y+1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{4}((y+1)^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{4}(2y+1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[{y}^{2}+y]}_{y=1}^{y=3} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(9+3)-\frac{1}{4}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-161581.name: Question 4
q-161581.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}y\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le y+z+2\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the $z$-axis and the line $z=2-y$ in the first quadrant.
q-161581.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z+2}y\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z+2}y\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}y[x]_{x=0}^{x=y+z+2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}y(y+z+2)\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14231356/assets/b473cc75dbbd6fa36ba43f6bbdec4a0133164e6fd8bc5f76ff86cec74714a256.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2-y}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2-y}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[({y}^{2}+2y)z+\frac{1}{2}y{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2-y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}+2y)(2-y)+\frac{1}{2}y(2-y)^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4y-{y}^{3})+\frac{1}{2}y(4-4y+{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}-2{y}^{2}+6y\,dy \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{8}{y}^{4}-\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+3{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =-2-\frac{16}{3}+12 \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-161592.name: Question 5
q-161592.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14231356/assets/f2f91e4ee1a90e1afb00d2f212e057235afe5c4e9089679da3af244c1d324676.png)

Evaluate the triple integral 
${∭}_{R}12x\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*
q-161592.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14231356/assets/b7e71e46310b065e2c03b4a0aebaa96268136c7f633eea6983612297e56361d1.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 1+y+z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14231356/assets/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 1+y+z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}12x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1+y+z}12x\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1+y+z}12x\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1+y+z}12x\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[6{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=1+y+z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}6(1+y+z)^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2}+12yz+12y+12z)\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2}+12yz+12y+12z)\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2}+12yz+12y+12z)\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[6z+6{y}^{2}z+2{z}^{3}+6y{z}^{2}+12yz+6{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+2+6y+12y+6)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6{y}^{2}+18y+14)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6{y}^{2}+18y+14)\,dy & =[2{y}^{3}+9{y}^{2}+14y]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(2+9+14)-0 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Evaluate the triple integral ∭R12xdV over the region R, shown above.

Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.

a
25
b
15
c
18
d
30
e
12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,0≤x≤1+y+z},

where

D={(y,z):0≤y≤1,0≤z≤1}

is the projection of R onto the yz-plane, shown below.

Hence, we can express the region R as

R={(x,y,z):0≤y≤1,0≤z≤1,0≤x≤1+y+z}

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

∭R12xdV=∫01∫01∫01+y+z12xdxdzdy.

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to x, treating y and z as constants:

∫01∫01∫01+y+z12xdxdzdy=∫01∫01[∫01+y+z12xdx]dzdy=∫01∫01[6x2]x=0x=1+y+zdzdy=∫01∫016(1+y+z)2dzdy=∫01∫01(6+6y2+6z2+12yz+12y+12z)dzdy

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to z, treating y as a constant:

∫01∫01(6+6y2+6z2+12yz+12y+12z)dzdy=∫01[∫01(6+6y2+6z2+12yz+12y+12z)dz]dy=∫01[6z+6y2z+2z3+6yz2+12yz+6z2]z=0z=1dy=∫01(6+6y2+2+6y+12y+6)dy=∫01(6y2+18y+14)dy

Finally, we integrate with respect to y:

∫01(6y2+18y+14)dy=[2y3+9y2+14y]y=0y=1=(2+9+14)−0=25.
